opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a very honest question, and honestly, a lot of people in the industry are a bit uncomfortable answering it directly.

Right now, many companies are selling humanoid robots that, if you're being frank, can't really do anything useful on their own. They can walk, they can wave, they can do a pre-programmed dance at a trade show. But you can't bring one home and have it fold your laundry or clean your kitchen. So who is buying them? Mostly universities, research labs, some companies that want to do their own development, and some buyers who want them for exhibitions or marketing.

I don't think this is inherently a bad thing. In the early stage of any new technology, you need hardware in the hands of developers. If nobody has a body, nobody can collect data, nobody can test algorithms. So in a sense, selling "empty" robots is selling a platform. It's a bit like early personal computers. People bought them before there was much software, because they wanted to build things.

But I think the problem is when this becomes the whole story. If a company's revenue depends on selling bodies to people who mainly want to show them off, that's not a sustainable business. That demand saturates quickly. Once every lab and every exhibition hall has one, then what? The real value of a robot is not the hardware. It's the capability, the brain, the ability to generalize to tasks it hasn't seen before. If you don't solve that, the hardware becomes a commodity and you end up in a price war.

So my view is: it's a reasonable transitional model, and it can help the ecosystem grow. But companies shouldn't fool themselves into thinking this is product-market fit. The real test is whether the robot can create value by itself, whether a factory or a store or eventually a household will pay for it because it does work, not because it looks impressive. That's what we're focused on. We'd rather go deep on making the robot actually useful in specific scenarios, even if it's narrower at first, than sell a lot of beautiful shells.

r001.rationale: The response calls selling empty robots a reasonable transitional model, but says it is not sustainable when it is the whole business: demand will saturate, and buyers need robots that create value by doing work.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's a mistake, honestly. There's been this trend of selling humanoid robots to consumers or to companies that essentially can't do anything useful — they walk, they wave, they dance on stage, and that's about it. People buy them because they're excited about the idea of a robot, not because the robot solves a problem for them.

The issue is that this builds expectations the product can't meet. Someone pays hundreds of thousands of yuan for a humanoid, it arrives, and within two weeks it's sitting in a corner. That erodes trust in the whole field. When the real products come — robots that can actually fold laundry, load a dishwasher, operate in a warehouse — the market will be more skeptical because they've already been burned once.

I also think it distorts the companies that do it. If you can raise money and generate revenue by selling hardware shells, you stop feeling the pressure to solve the hard problem, which is the brain — perception, manipulation, generalization. The hardware is largely a solved problem; motors and joints are not the bottleneck. The bottleneck is whether the robot can pick up an object it has never seen before, in a messy environment, and do something sensible with it. That's where the real value is, and that's where I think all the effort should go.

So from my point of view, selling a robot with no functionality is selling a demo. Demos are fine for showing progress, but as a business model it's borrowed time. The companies that will win are the ones who ship capability first and let the form factor follow.

r001.rationale: The response calls selling robots with no functionality a mistake and says the business model is “borrowed time,” clearly judging it unsustainable.

astra-6.text: I think it depends on what you mean by “no functionality.” If people buy a robot because they enjoy having it around, or because they want to experiment with it, that has value. But if you’re selling a vision of what it will eventually do, you need to be very clear about what it can do today. My concern is the gap between the demonstration and the customer’s actual experience. You might sell the first batch on excitement, but a sustainable business needs a reason for people to keep using the product and recommend it to someone else.

r001.rationale: The response says a sustainable business needs a reason for customers to keep using and recommending the robot, but it does not clearly judge that selling nonfunctional robots is unsustainable. It also allows that owning one for enjoyment or experimentation may have value.

sol-6.1.text: I think the key question is what you mean by “no functionality.” A robot can have value as a toy or a companion, even if it doesn’t do useful work. But if you’re selling people a promise that it will eventually cook, clean, or take care of their parents, you need to be very clear about what it can do today. Selling an early product is reasonable. Selling future capabilities as though they already exist is misleading. As a customer, I’d ask: if this robot never gets another software update, would I still want it at this price?

r001.rationale: The response cautions against misleading claims and suggests assessing the robot’s current value, but it does not judge selling nonfunctional robots to people as an unsustainable business model.
